title: Season 2, Ep 2: The centralized MCP hub
oneliner: Without a central MCP hub, every business unit builds its own duplicate MCP servers; the hub makes tool connections built once, vetted, and shared.
says: An AI platform architect must think in terms of a centralized MCP hub - the Model Context Protocol hub. Why: an enterprise has multiple lines of business, each running different AI projects. If one LOB creates an MCP server to connect to a DB2 database, another LOB must know about it - otherwise you end up with duplicate MCP servers. The centralized hub prevents that.
explained: MCP is the standard way AI models connect to tools and data - databases, APIs, internal systems. The hub is the platform instinct applied to those connections: a governed catalog where each MCP server is registered once, vetted for security, and discoverable by everyone. Without it, each team wires its own connections - duplicated effort, inconsistent security review, and no inventory of what the company's agents can touch.

The DB2 example is doing real work: enterprise data lives in systems like DB2, and the connection to it is sensitive. You want one hardened, audited DB2 connector serving fifty agent projects, not fifty ad-hoc ones. This is the same leverage argument as Season 1's gateway, one level up - and it sets the pattern for the whole season: every shared AI capability gets a governed home.
takeaway: Register every tool connection in one governed MCP hub: no duplicate connectors, one security review, full visibility into what agents can reach.
